opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think research taste is one of the most important and also one of the most mysterious skills in research. When I say "taste," I roughly mean the intuitions that guide your decisions: which problems are worth working on, which experiments to run next, when to give up on a direction, when something is interesting versus a distraction, and when a result is actually convincing versus when you're fooling yourself.

The thing I'd emphasize for people who are new is that taste is mostly learned through feedback loops, and the core problem is that those loops are really slow. If your unit of feedback is "I picked a research project, worked on it for six months, and it did or didn't pan out," you might get a handful of data points in your first couple of years. That's not enough to learn much. So a lot of my advice is about finding ways to get faster, denser feedback.

A few concrete things. First, I think you should explicitly not expect to have good taste at the start, and that's fine. When I mentor people, I often tell them: for your first project, don't worry too much about picking the perfect problem. Take something a more experienced person thinks is reasonable, and focus on learning the more tactical skills, like writing code quickly, running experiments, and reading your data carefully. Those have much tighter feedback loops, and they're a prerequisite anyway. You can't really judge which ideas are good if you can't execute on them yet.

Second, you can learn from other people's taste much faster than from your own experience. Work with a mentor, and when they make a call, like "let's drop this" or "this result is suspicious," ask them why. Try to predict what they'll say before they say it, and notice when you're wrong. That's a really cheap feedback signal. Each conversation becomes a mini training example instead of one per six-month project.

Third, practise making predictions about your own research. Before you run an experiment, write down what you expect to happen and how confident you are. Then you find out, and you're calibrating your intuitions every day rather than every few months. A lot of people skip this because it feels like overhead, but I think it's one of the highest-leverage habits.

And finally, I'd encourage a lot of skepticism, especially in a field like interpretability, where it's very easy to tell yourself a compelling story about what a model is doing that turns out to be wrong. Good taste is partly having a well-tuned sense of "how could this be an illusion?" You build that by getting burned a few times, ideally on small things, and by reading work critically and asking what would have to be true for the claims to hold.

So the summary is: don't stress about having taste early. Get good at execution, borrow taste from people who have it, and deliberately create faster feedback loops so your intuitions actually have something to learn from.

r001.rationale: It defines taste as guiding several decisions, including what experiments to run, when to stop, and how to assess results, beyond choosing a project.

r002.rationale: It contrasts slow feedback from a six-month project with tighter feedback loops for tactical skills such as coding and running experiments.

r003.rationale: It recommends predicting experiment outcomes to calibrate intuitions, but does not frame taste development as predicting whether research questions will work out.

r004.rationale: It says taste is slow to learn because project feedback takes months, while tactical skills have tighter feedback loops.

r005.rationale: It recommends focusing first on execution skills such as coding, running experiments, and reading data.

r006.rationale: It advises taking a reasonable project chosen by an experienced person and learning from a mentor's judgments while building execution skills.

r007.rationale: It does not recommend using unambitious projects when a mentor is unavailable.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the most important questions, and also one where people often get a slightly wrong model of what's going on.

So research taste is this kind of nebulous thing — the ability to look at a problem and have good intuitions about which directions are promising, which experiments are worth running, when a result is actually interesting versus when you're fooling yourself, when to give up on something. And the frustrating thing is that it's largely tacit knowledge. It's not the kind of thing you can read a textbook on. It's much more like learning to ride a bike, or learning a language: you get it by doing a lot of reps and getting feedback.

And I think the key mistake people make is thinking of it as some innate property, like "do I have taste or not?" It's a skill. It's learned. The people who have great taste are mostly people who have spent years doing research, making lots of mistakes, and slowly building up a library of patterns. The first time you waste three months on a project that was doomed from the start, that's painful, but you learn something you'll carry forward forever.

So what does that imply practically if you're new? A few things.

First, you need to actually do research. Not read about research, not plan to do research — do it. Pick a small, concrete project and just start. A lot of people get stuck in this mode of "I need to understand the whole field before I can contribute," and that's mostly wrong. Understanding comes from engaging with real problems.

Second, you want fast feedback loops. The reason mentorship is so valuable is that a good mentor can compress the feedback cycle enormously. Instead of spending three months discovering a direction is a dead end, someone with taste can tell you in five minutes. So if you can find a mentor, or even just people with more experience who'll look at your ideas and tell you honestly what they think, that's incredibly high leverage. And you should actively solicit criticism, not just validation.

Third, and this is something I feel strongly about: try to make your own predictions and then check them. Before you run an experiment, write down what you expect to see. Before you read the methods section of a paper, guess what approach they took. Before your mentor gives feedback, guess what they'll say. You basically want to be constantly running your own intuitions against reality, so you can notice where they're miscalibrated. That's how you turn experience into taste, rather than just experience.

Fourth, I'd say lean towards doing lots of small, fast projects early on rather than one big ambitious one. Each project is a chance to learn about the full cycle: picking a question, trying things, hitting walls, figuring out what the result actually means. If you do a big project, you get one rep. If you do five small ones, you get five, and you'll learn a lot more about which kinds of problems are tractable.

And then the last thing is, I think there's a certain amount of just... being okay with being confused and wrong for a while. Everyone's early research is kind of bad. Mine was. That's fine. The goal isn't to be good immediately; it's to be the kind of person who learns quickly from being bad. If you go in with that mindset, the whole thing is a lot less stressful, and honestly you progress faster too, because you're not paralysed by trying to avoid mistakes that are basically unavoidable.

r001.rationale: It describes taste as judging promising directions, experiments, whether results are interesting, and when to give up, covering decisions beyond project choice.

r002.rationale: It discusses speeding up feedback with a mentor, but does not say feedback loops differ in duration across research skills.

r003.rationale: It recommends making predictions and checking them against reality, and describes taste as judging which directions are promising and which problems are tractable.

r004.rationale: It says taste takes years to develop, but does not compare its pace with the development of easier research skills.

r005.rationale: It does not recommend learning other research skills before focusing on taste.

r006.rationale: It recommends getting mentor feedback to shorten feedback cycles, but does not frame this as relying on the mentor's taste while developing other research skills.

r007.rationale: It recommends small projects generally, but does not tie that recommendation to practicing when a mentor is unavailable.

astra-6.text:
I think research taste is basically your ability to look at a question and predict whether spending time on it will teach you something useful. And when you’re new, you shouldn’t expect to be very good at that. Part of the point of doing research is to develop that judgment.

One thing I’d recommend is making your predictions explicit. Before you start a project, write down: Why do I think this is interesting? What do I expect to happen? What would I learn if it didn’t happen? Then, after you’ve worked on it for a bit, go back and compare. Did you actually resolve the uncertainty you cared about? Or did you spend a week getting some code to run and lose track of what question you were asking?

I’d also favour short projects with quick feedback. You can learn a lot from taking a question, trying the simplest experiment you can think of, and discovering that your framing was confused. That’s a useful outcome, especially if it takes two days rather than six months.

And talk to experienced researchers. But don’t just ask, ‘Is this a good idea?’ Ask what makes them excited or sceptical, and try to understand the reasoning. Ideally, form your own view first, so you can notice where their judgment differs from yours.

The thing I’d push against is waiting until you have good taste before you start. You develop it by making choices, seeing what happens, and reflecting on why.

r001.rationale: It discusses choosing and evaluating projects, but does not say research taste applies to decisions at multiple levels within research.

r002.rationale: It recommends short projects with quick feedback, but does not identify that different research skills have feedback loops of different durations.

r003.rationale: It defines taste as predicting whether a question will teach something useful, not as predicting whether the research question will work out.

r004.rationale: It says beginners should not expect to be good at research taste, but does not compare its development speed with that of easier research skills.

r005.rationale: It argues against waiting to develop taste before starting research; it does not recommend learning other research skills first.

r006.rationale: It recommends asking experienced researchers for their reasoning, but does not suggest relying on a mentor's taste while developing other skills.

r007.rationale: It recommends short projects for quick feedback, but does not recommend unambitious projects to practise skills when a mentor is unavailable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think research taste is partly about having good intuitions for which questions are important, which are tractable, and which experiments will actually teach you something. And when you’re starting out, you shouldn’t expect to have particularly good intuitions about all of those things. That’s a lot of what you’re there to learn.

One thing I’d encourage is making your predictions explicit. Before you run an experiment, write down what you think will happen and why. Then, when you get the result, ask what you got wrong. Did you misunderstand the model? Was the experiment poorly designed? Was your hypothesis too vague to really be tested? You get much more out of an experiment if you can compare the result to an actual expectation, rather than retrospectively thinking, “Oh, yeah, that makes sense.”

I also think it’s useful to work with someone whose research taste you respect, but to ask them for their reasoning. If they say a project seems promising, what makes it promising? What would make them abandon it? You want to learn how they make those judgments, and then practise making the judgments yourself.

And I’d favour short feedback loops early on. Find a small question, try to answer it, and see whether the answer changes how you think. You don’t need your first project to be incredibly important. You need it to give you useful feedback, so that your next choice of project is a bit better informed.

r001.rationale: The response applies research taste to judging which questions matter, which are tractable, and which experiments will teach something—not just to choosing projects.

r002.rationale: It recommends short feedback loops early on but does not compare feedback-loop durations across different research skills.

r003.rationale: It discusses intuitions about importance and tractability and predicting experiment results, but does not frame taste development as predicting whether research questions will work out.

r004.rationale: It says beginners should not expect strong intuitions yet, but does not say taste develops more slowly than easier research skills.

r005.rationale: It does not recommend learning other research skills before focusing on research taste.

r006.rationale: It recommends learning from someone whose taste the beginner respects, but does not say to rely on that mentor's taste while developing other research skills.

r007.rationale: It recommends starting with a small question, but does not link unambitious projects to practising research skills when a mentor is unavailable.
